title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling Playbooks, Benchmarks, and Runbooks
author: Priya Natarajan
content:
Overview

This document consolidates the serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling policies, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, release notes summary, known issues, and operational runbooks. It is intended as the single source of truth for engineers and SREs who operate or extend the Redwood serving runtime (services: rdrw-runtime, rdrw-scheduler, rdrw-batcher, rdrw-cache, rdrw-inspector). Use linked runbooks for one-off incident procedures.

Goals and scope
- Provide a high-level architecture and component responsibilities.
- Define kernel scheduling classes and configuration used in production.
- Describe standardized profiling steps and tooling for performance triage.
- Document benchmarking suite and metrics we track.
- Summarize recent runtime releases and behavioral changes.
- Capture known issues and recommended mitigations.
- Include runbooks for common operational tasks and escalations.

1) Runtime architecture (summary)

High-level components
- rdrw-runtime: the main inference process (C++/CUDA) that hosts model weights, executes kernels, and exposes a gRPC HTTP/REST front-end.
- rdrw-scheduler: policy engine that routes requests to nodes and decides kernel selection and KV cache reuse.
- rdrw-batcher: continuous batching layer that aggregates requests while honoring latency SLOs.
- rdrw-cache: prefix/KV cache service with sharding by model-version.
- rdrw-inspector: observability sidecar that collects perf counters and traces.

Responsibilities and data flow
1. API request arrives at load balancer -> routed to rdrw-router (edge).
2. rdrw-router consults rdrw-scheduler for target model-version and node affinity.
3. Request flows to rdrw-batcher on chosen node; batcher decides grouping based on QoS class and historical latency.
4. Batcher calls rdrw-runtime with batched input; runtime picks kernel plan and executes on GPU.
5. Outputs are de-batched and returned; key metrics and traces sent to rdrw-inspector.

SLOs and service-level metrics
- Latency targets (hosted tier): p50 <= 35ms, p95 <= 80ms, p99 <= 150ms for text-generation requests with max_output_tokens=64 on common small models.
- Throughput: per-GPU steady-state target 2.5k tokens/s for gpt-small-class models (quantized int8) under throughput workloads.
- Error rate: <0.1% 5xx for steady-state traffic.
- Availability: 99.95% monthly for dedicated clusters.

Ownership
- Runtime core: serving-runtime team.
- Scheduler and batching policies: serving-runtime team + infra-platform for capacity rules.
- Observability/Inspector: eng-platform.

2) Kernel selection and scheduling policy

Overview
Kernel selection is performed inside rdrw-runtime prior to execution. The selection algorithm balances three dimensions: latency, throughput (GPU utilization), and memory footprint. Kernels are tagged in our internal catalog with attributes: arch, precision (fp16/int8), workspace_bytes, tile_shape, expected_latency_per_token.

QoS classes
1. latency-sensitive: smallest batch sizes, lowest queuing, favor low-latency kernels (no aggressive fusion), always use preemptible low-latency CUDA stream.
2. balanced: default for most tenants — medium batch windows and adaptive kernel selection.
3. throughput-optimized: larger batch windows, prefer kernels with higher utilization even if p99 latency increases.
4. background: model warmers, re-encodings, offline tasks with low priority.

Policy knobs (configurable via /etc/rdrw/scheduler.conf or dynamic via API)
- max_batch_window_ms: how long batcher waits (per QoS). Typical values: latency-sensitive=8ms, balanced=25ms, throughput-optimized=75ms.
- kernel_latency_threshold_ms: reject kernels whose expected latency per token exceeds configured value for QoS.
- memory_headroom_ratio: fraction of GPU memory to keep free for preemption (default 0.12).
- preemption_enabled: true/false.

Kernel selection logic (simplified)
1. Candidate kernels = kernels compatible with model architecture and precision.
2. Filter if workspace_bytes > available_workspace.
3. Rank by score = w1*(1/expected_latency) + w2*(throughput_score) - w3*(workspace_bytes_ratio). Weights are QoS-specific.
4. Select top candidate; if preemption_enabled and predicted_p99 > SLO, fallback to lower-precision or smaller-tile kernels.

Example kernel config table (ASCII):
Name | precision | tile | workspace_bytes | expected_ms_per_token | tags
fast-attn-64 | fp16 | 64x64 | 256MB | 0.4 | latency, small-seq
util-attn-128 | fp16 | 128x128 | 700MB | 0.8 | throughput
quant-attn-8  | int8 | 128x128 | 420MB | 1.1 | quantized, throughput

3) Profiling playbook (triage and routine profiling)

When to profile
- Regressions: increased p95/p99 latency, drop in tokens/s, increased GPU memory OOM.
- New model onboarding: collect baseline traces on representative traffic.
- Kernel/evaluator changes: verify expected perf improvements.

Tools we use
- rdrw-profiler (internal) — collects per-kernel timelines, CUDA kernel durations, and memory metric snapshots.
- nvprof/ncu (NVIDIA Nsight CLI) for deep kernel analysis.
- perf/top and flamegraphs for CPU-side hotspots.
- eBPF traces for system-level latency sources (rdrw-ebpf).

Standard profiling steps
1. Reproduce with a controlled load: run benchmark-client against isolated node with same model-version and config. Use the benchmark suite (see section 4).
2. Capture steady-state traces: start rdrw-profiler with --duration 60s and representative prompt mix.
3. Inspect per-kernel durations and utilization. Look for kernels with high variance (sigma/mean > 0.35) — these indicate queuing jitter or memory migration.
4. If GPU stalls are observed, collect ncu timeline and check for PCIe or NVLink stalls.
5. Validate batcher behavior: ensure batch sizes match QoS expectations and that batching wait windows are not being exceeded.
6. Collect and correlate infra metrics (GPU temp, power, CPU steal, host network drop).

Quick commands (examples)
- Start profiling: rdrw-profiler --node-id node-42 --model-model:v2 --duration 60 --output /tmp/prof.json
- Run micro-benchmark: python -m rdrw.bench.client --model model:v2 --qos latency-sensitive --concurrency 8 --prompts-file samples.json

4) Benchmarking suite and CI integration

Purpose
- Provide reproducible, versioned performance baselines for each model-version and runtime release.
- Separate benchmarks: latency suite (small sequences), throughput suite (long sequences), memory/scale tests.

Components
- benchctl: CLI to run scenarios, collect traces, and upload results to bench-store.
- bench-store: time-series store for bench runs with metadata (cloud region, GPU type, quantization).
- regression-alerts: scheduled job that compares latest bench runs to baseline and opens an issue when regressions exceed thresholds.

Standard scenarios
- latency-short: 8-token prompt, max_output_tokens=64, concurrency sweep 1..16.
- throughput-long: 512-context, continuous streaming 4 clients, measure tokens/s for 5 minutes.
- memory-stress: synthetic large-batch to exercise workspace and KV cache.

Bench metrics we store (string keys):
- bench.latency.p50, bench.latency.p95, bench.latency.p99
- bench.throughput.tokens_per_second
- bench.gpu.utilization.mean, bench.gpu.utilization.p95
- bench.gpu.memory.peak_bytes

CI hooks
- Every merge to main triggers benchctl-run for a set of smoke scenarios in a GPU staging pool. Results are compared against the baseline for the current release branch.
- Nightly: full benchmark suite across representative GPU types (A800, H100s, V100).

5) Release notes summary (last 6 months)

v2026.10.3 (2026-12-15) — production roll
- Improved kernel fallback for quantized models; 8–12% throughput improvement on baseline prompts.
- Default batch_window reduced for latency-sensitive QoS from 12ms -> 8ms.
- Fix: avoid double-free on model reload edge-case.

v2026.07.1 (2026-07-14)
- Introduced memory_headroom_ratio and dynamic preemption flag.
- Added benchctl integration to PR pipeline.

v2026.04.22 (2026-04-22)
- rdarw-scheduler refactor: node scoring now includes cache hit probability.

Upgrade guidance
- Rolling upgrade: drain nodes using /api/v1/admin/drain, wait for in-flight requests to complete, verify bench latency on drained nodes before re-introducing. See runbook below.

6) Known issues & mitigations

Issue: p99 spikes when GPU memory fragmentation occurs
- Symptoms: sudden p99 latency increase without sustained GPU utilization rise.
- Root cause: frequent model loads/unloads increase fragmentation of CUDA workspace pools.
- Mitigation: enable workspace pooling (default enabled) and increase memory_headroom_ratio to 0.18 for busy nodes. Scheduled long-term fix: runtime-level heap compacting in v2027.

Issue: occasional NVLink transfer stalls on mixed-generation NVLink topologies
- Symptoms: long tail seen in nvprof with periodic stalls.
- Mitigation: pin heavy cross-GPU KV-cache traffic to NVLink-local replicas; configure scheduler to prefer intra-socket-same-pod routing.

Issue: quantized kernels show higher variance on long-context workloads
- Symptoms: p95 variance increases for throughput tests > 1024 tokens.
- Mitigation: use hybrid kernel strategy: run first 512 tokens on fp16 kernel then switch to int8 for remaining tokens. Flag: --hybrid-kernel-strategy (runtime opt-in).

7) Runbooks (common operational procedures)

A) Node drain and rolling upgrade (owner: eng-sre)
1. Identify node: node-42 requires upgrade.
2. Mark node drain: curl -X POST https://internal.api/admin/nodes/node-42/drain -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN"
3. Monitor /metrics for inflight_requests on node-42 until zero (expect <120s for idle nodes).
4. Run benchctl smoke against node-42: benchctl --node node-42 --scenario latency-short. Compare against baseline.
5. Upgrade package: sudo dpkg -i /releases/rdrw-runtime-v2026.10.3.deb
6. Start service and run quick healthcheck: systemctl start rdrw-runtime; curl -f http://localhost:8080/healthz
7. Run benchctl smoke again; if regressions exceed 5% p95, rollback and open ticket: #runtime-regressions.
8. Un-drain node: curl -X POST https://internal.api/admin/nodes/node-42/undrain

B) Kernel fallback trigger (owner: serving-runtime)
1. Detect regression via regression-alerts or manual observation.
2. Switch QoS weight to favor latency by setting qos.weights in dynamic config: payload {"balanced":{"w1":0.65,"w2":0.25,"w3":0.1}} via API.
3. If emergency, force-apply conservative kernel list: POST /api/v1/admin/kernel-policy with policy=conservative.
4. Run profiler and attach traces to the incident.

C) Emergency capacity scaling (owner: eng-platform)
1. If nodes hit >85% memory/headroom or GPU util >94% sustained, trigger burst pool: terraform apply with var.enable_burst=true (infra-approved runbook required).
2. Validate scheduler is honoring new capacity by checking scheduler.metrics.nodes_active_count.

8) Team wiki & docs links (quick references)
- Architecture deep-dive: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/serving-runtime-architecture-playbook-2026-03-01
- Profiling CLI docs: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/serving-runtime-profiling-benchmarks-2026
- Benchstore dashboards: https://benchstore.internal.redwood/
- Incident channel: #runtime-ops on Slack (pager: runtime-oncall)

Appendix A: Example dynamic scheduler.conf (YAML snippet)

# scheduler.conf snippet
qos:
  latency-sensitive:
    max_batch_window_ms: 8
    kernel_latency_threshold_ms: 0.6
  balanced:
    max_batch_window_ms: 25
    kernel_latency_threshold_ms: 1.2
  throughput-optimized:
    max_batch_window_ms: 75
    kernel_latency_threshold_ms: 2.5
memory_headroom_ratio: 0.12
preemption_enabled: true

Appendix B: Troubleshooting checklist (one-line steps)
- Reproduce on isolated node with benchctl.
- Run rdrw-profiler for 60s.
- Check batcher wait windows and average batch sizes.
- Inspect kernel timelines for variance.
- Validate GPU memory and PCIe/NVLink metrics.
- If urgent, switch to conservative kernel policy and scale burst pool.

Contact and escalation
- Primary oncall: runtime-oncall (contact via pagerduty)
- Owner: serving-runtime team (serving-runtime@redwood.internal)
- Escalate to eng-platform for infra-level issues (eng-platform@redwood.internal)
